claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain and toughness than commercially pure tungsten.
The proposed improvement in plastic strain and toughness is governed by lattice distortion in the multi-principal-element solid solution.
Lattice distortion activates additional dislocation slip systems in WTaTiVZr.
Additional slip systems promote more homogeneous plastic flow in WTaTiVZr.
As-sintered equimolar WTaTiVZr has a primarily BCC single-phase microstructure.
As-sintered WTaTiVZr may contain minor secondary phases.
Temperatures approaching 1000 °C are relevant to plasma-facing-component service.
Multiple refractory elements produce local variations in atomic spacing and barrier fields for dislocation motion.
Multi-principal alloying in WTaTiVZr increases solid-solution strengthening.
Heterogeneous lattice strains modify dislocation nucleation and propagation.
Modified dislocation behavior activates additional slip systems and distributes plastic deformation.
Distributed plastic deformation improves energy absorption and toughness.
Pure tungsten lacks the microstructural complexity attributed to WTaTiVZr.
Under identical high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will have a lower yield stress than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will have significantly greater plastic strain and fracture strain than pure tungsten.
Under identical high-temperature testing, WTaTiVZr will resist crack propagation better than pure tungsten.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate where dislocation mobility is thermally activated and the alloy remains phase-stable.
Significant secondary phases or grain-boundary precipitates could cause the proposed mechanism not to dominate.

contradictions.description: The mechanism invokes increased solid-solution strengthening, while the predicted outcome is a lower yield stress than pure tungsten. These directions are in tension and no temperature-dependent softening or other competing effect is specified to reconcile them.
